paras: The whipping of Richard Hindsman was an assault in Villa Rica, Georgia, reported on August 9, 1885, in which white residents described as "indignant white citizens" gave a Black man three hundred lashes on the claim that he had insulted a white woman. The coverage consisted of a single Atlanta dispatch reprinted across the country, and it reports no arrests or legal proceedings. The case drew an editorial from the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer, which condemned the whipping as a usurpation of the law and an instance of unequal justice for Black people.

The report began as a special dispatch to the Atlanta Constitution and was relayed by telegraph from Atlanta under the date August 9, 1885; the Omaha Daily Bee printed it with a Villa Rica dateline. The coverage says nothing about the alleged insult, the woman involved, or what led up to the whipping.

According to the dispatch, Richard Hindsman, described as "colored," was accused of insulting "a white lady" and was then given three hundred lashes by "indignant white citizens" of the town. The wire stated as fact that he "was guilty of insulting" her, though it mentions no hearing; in rewording it, the Concord People and Patriot wrote that he was "charged with" the insult, while the National Tribune said he was "proved guilty." None of the reports names the men who did the whipping, gives their number, says where in the town it took place, or describes his injuries.

No report of an arrest, inquest, indictment or other official action against the men who whipped Hindsman was found in the coverage. The only response the papers record was editorial: on August 11 the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer argued that Georgia law did not provide for such a punishment and that the citizens had no right to act in its place.

The dispatch ran in white newspapers from August 10 to August 21, 1885, almost always as a single sentence in a column of telegrams or crime notes. On August 10 alone it appeared in the New-York Tribune, the Washington Evening Star, the St. Paul Daily Globe, the Springfield Globe-Republic, the Fort Worth Daily Gazette, the Dallas Daily Herald and the Wheeling Register. Over the next eleven days it reached the Omaha Daily Bee, the Delaware Gazette and weeklies from Kentucky and Tennessee to Vermont and Dakota.

Headlines varied in tone: the New-York Tribune used "Three Hundred Lashes Given a Negro" and the Fort Worth Daily Gazette "The Whipping Post Revived," while the Dallas Daily Herald headed the item with the jocular They "Tickled His Ribs." Most papers repeated the wire's wording unaltered, including its statement that Hindsman "was guilty" and its description of the whippers as "indignant white citizens." The Springfield Globe-Republic printed it directly above a report of the Cuthbert, Georgia, lynching of Henry Davis headed "Deservedly Lynched," and the Omaha Daily Bee ran it beneath the Cuthbert story under "Georgia Justice."

The Wheeling Daily Intelligencer's editorial "A Peace Issue" put "indignant white citizens" in quotation marks and declared that "Citizens, white or black, hav. no right to usurp the authority of Judge, Jury and Sheriff." It argued that a white man who insulted a white woman would not have been "tied at a lamp-post and lashed on the spot," and that whatever equal justice existed on the statute books "stops there," with "the black people" paying for the difference. It called the matter "purely a peace question" rather than a sectional issue, and it was the only commentary found; no coverage appeared in the Black papers searched.

The victim's name appears as Hindsman in most papers but as "Hindman" in the Omaha Daily Bee, "Hindeman" in the New-York Tribune, "Henderson" in the St. Paul Daily Globe and "Anderson" in the Griggs Courier of Dakota. All of these carry the same wording and describe one man. The number of lashes is also inconsistent: every other version gives three hundred, but the Burlington Weekly Free Press printed "thirty lashes" under the heading "A Negro Lashed Thirty Times" while otherwise repeating the Constitution special word for word. The lamp-post detail in the Wheeling editorial does not appear in any wire version found.

accounts.label: Atlanta Constitution special (wire report)
accounts.gist: Richard Hindsman, colored, of Villa Rica, 'who was guilty of insulting a white lady', was given 300 lashes by 'indignant white citizens'; the accusation is stated as fact and no source for it is given.

accounts.label: Wheeling Daily Intelligencer editorial
accounts.gist: Restating the wire, the paper said citizens had no right to usurp judge, jury and sheriff, that no state punished an insult with 300 lashes, and that a white man would not have been 'tied at a lamp-post and lashed on the spot'.

framing.detail: Headline 'Three Hundred Lashes Given a Negro'; repeats the Constitution dispatch that he 'was guilty' and the whippers were 'indignant white citizens'.
Printed under 'Given Three Hundred Lashes' directly above a Cuthbert, Ga., lynching item headed 'Deservedly Lynched'.
Jocular headline They "Tickled His Ribs." over the unaltered wire text.
Headline 'The Whipping Post Revived' over the Atlanta special.
Crime-column brief recasting the claim as 'charged with insulting a white lady'.
Editorial 'A Peace Issue': citizens have no right to 'usurp the authority of Judge, Jury and Sheriff'; equal justice 'stops there' at the statute books 'and the black people pay for it'.

conflicts.note: All versions carry the same wording and describe one man; the variants are spelling or transmission errors in a single wire item, Hindsman being the most common form.
The Burlington weekly otherwise repeats the Constitution special word for word; every other opened version gives 300. Search-excerpt OCR readings of 500 and 800 were 300 on re-read.
All rewordings of the same dispatch; none reports a hearing or any proof.
